questions.prompt: In discovery, a MindBody studio owner says her contract “renews sometime in the fall.” What's your best next move?

options.text: Ask her to check the exact date and notice period before you go on
Note it as fall and bring timing up again once pricing comes up
Tell her to cancel MindBody now so the renewal can't catch her out
Skip it, since timing only matters once she has picked her plan

questions.reveal: “Sometime in the fall” can't anchor a close. The exact date and notice period can.

questions.prompt: Why ask about the current contract in discovery instead of at the close?

options.text: It shows whether she can afford Momence before you share pricing
The renewal date sets the deadline you plan the whole switch around
Prospects only answer contract questions before they've seen price
It tells you which competitor she'll most likely compare you with

questions.reveal: Asked early, the date shapes the whole call. Found at the end, it's a surprise that stalls the deal.

questions.prompt: A prospect's contract renews soon and she'd pay for both systems while she onboards. She asks if you can cover the overlap. What do you do?

options.text: Promise her free months to cover the overlap so she signs today
Tell her the overlap is normal and every new customer pays both
Ask your manager what you can offer, then put it in the agreement
Advise her to renew her old contract and switch next year instead

questions.reveal: Covering an overlap is a concession. It needs approval, and once approved it goes in writing.

questions.prompt: A prospect has no contract with her current system and says she'll “switch in the new year.” What's the strongest move?

options.text: Accept the timeline and set a reminder to call her in late December
Offer a discount that only applies if she signs before the new year
Tell her a studio with no contract should always switch right away
Work back from her go-live date and agree when she needs to sign

questions.reveal: Her go-live date is the deadline. Onboarding and migration take time, so the signing date comes well before it.

questions.prompt: Near the end of a demo, the prospect says, “I'm seeing Arketa tomorrow.” What should you do before the call ends?

options.text: List what Arketa can't do so she can ask them about each one
Book a follow-up for after Arketa and ask what she'll compare
Offer a price that only holds if she cancels the Arketa demo
Tell her to reach out after Arketa if she has more questions

questions.reveal: Know what she'll weigh and be the first call after the other demo.

questions.prompt: A prospect names a real strength of a competitor she's also seeing. What's the right stance?

options.text: Question the claim and ask where she heard it before you move on
Change the subject back to the features you planned to show next
Acknowledge the strength, then show where Momence is stronger for her
Agree, then offer a discount to make up for the gap in features

questions.reveal: Conceding a real strength builds trust. Then tie Momence's strengths to what she said matters.

questions.prompt: Forty minutes in, the owner mentions her husband “handles the money side” and hasn't seen anything yet. What do you do?

options.text: Give her a pricing sheet she can walk him through on her own tonight
Ask her to sign now, since she's the one running the studio each day
Leave it with her and wait to hear back once the two of them talk
Offer a short call with both of them and send him the agreement too

questions.reveal: The person who decides should hear it from you, and every signer should have the agreement.

questions.prompt: A studio has three owners who all sign. When the agreement goes out, who should get it?

options.text: Every owner who signs, along with the recap or the recording
Only your main contact, so the others hear it from her first
Only the owner who handles money, since that's who decides
Nobody yet; wait until all three have seen a demo with you

questions.reveal: Sending it to everyone who signs keeps the deal from waiting on one person to forward it.

questions.prompt: You ask to book a follow-up. The prospect says, “I'll check my calendar and email you a time.” What's best?

options.text: Send your booking link so she can pick a time when it suits her
Agree, and send a reminder email if you haven't heard in a week
Ask her to open her calendar now so you can pick the time together
Leave it with her, since pushing for a time can feel too pushy

questions.reveal: A time picked together on the call is a next step. A promise to email one is a hope.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a real next step?

options.text: I'll email the recap and touch base with you at the end of the week
Reach out whenever you've had a chance to look over the pricing
I'll send a calendar link so you can pick a time that suits you
Monday at 10:30 with both owners, to answer questions and decide

questions.reveal: A date, a time, the right people and a purpose. Everything else depends on someone remembering.

questions.prompt: The decision-maker is a general manager who wasn't on the call. Your contact meets him tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Book a call for after that meeting and invite the manager to join
Send a link so she can book time once the manager has decided
Ask her to forward your recap and let him reach out if he's keen
Push her to sign today so the manager doesn't need to be involved

questions.reveal: Tie the next step to the meeting that matters, and put the decision-maker on it.

questions.prompt: What makes a next step clear?

options.text: A recap email listing every feature you showed on the demo
A date, a time, who joins and what you'll decide on that call
A promise from the prospect to get back to you within a week
A pricing sheet and a link to your calendar to book a time

questions.reveal: If both sides can say what happens and when, it's a next step.

questions.prompt: While you walk the agreement, the prospect asks what happens to her price after the first year. The agreement doesn't say. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her prices never go up, since that's what you've heard on calls
Say it depends and move on so the question doesn't stall the close
Tell her she can renegotiate anything once her first year is done
Say you'll confirm with your manager and send the answer in writing

questions.reveal: If it isn't written in the agreement, don't state it from memory. Confirm it and put it in writing.

questions.prompt: The prospect asks, “So how long am I committed for?” The agreement is on screen. What do you do?

options.text: Show her the term as it's written in the agreement in front of her
Tell her the term other AEs usually quote on calls like this one
Say it's flexible, so the question doesn't slow down the signing
Tell her the term from the last agreement you sent to a studio

questions.reveal: State only the terms written in her agreement. Terms change, and hers is the one she's signing.

questions.prompt: A prospect asks you to push her first payment out by a couple of months. What do you do?

options.text: Agree on the call, since a later payment won't change the total
Check with your manager, then add any approved change in writing
Refuse, since payment dates can never move once a quote is out
Agree now and tell your manager once she has signed the agreement

questions.reveal: Payment timing is a concession. Get it approved first, then write it into the agreement.

questions.prompt: Your manager approves a concession. Where should it end up?

options.text: In the recap email, so she has a record of what you promised
In your CRM notes, so onboarding knows what you told the owner
Written into the agreement, so she sees it before she signs
Nowhere formal; you'll honor it when the account's billing starts

questions.reveal: An approved concession belongs in the agreement as an addendum, where both sides can see it.

questions.prompt: The prospect says yes but wants to sign the agreement “later tonight.” You want onboarding booked. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her to sign now while you're both on the call, so you can book
Book onboarding now and trust that she'll sign the agreement tonight
Thank her and wait for an email telling you the agreement is signed
Send a second copy of the agreement so it's at the top of her inbox

questions.reveal: Onboarding can't be booked until the agreement is signed. Signed live is signed.

questions.prompt: What has to be done before you can book a new customer's onboarding?

options.text: Signed agreement, a migration file and a launch date
Signed agreement, a host account and a card on file
A host account, a branded app and the first payment
A card on file and her old contract fully cancelled

questions.reveal: Agreement, host account and card on file come first. Onboarding gets booked after.

questions.prompt: Before she signs, a prospect says, “My old system just offered me a big discount to stay.” What do you do?

options.text: Match the discount right away so price is no longer a factor
Tell her the discount will disappear when her year is up anyway
Ask what made her start looking, and whether a discount fixes that
Say she should take it if price is the only thing that matters

questions.reveal: A retention discount changes the price, not the reasons she started looking. Bring her back to those.

questions.prompt: Why does the old system keep running until the switch date?

options.text: So the old vendor can migrate her data over to Momence for her
So she keeps a backup in case she decides to leave Momence later
So she avoids an early cancellation fee from the old vendor's side
So the studio keeps booking and taking payments while onboarding runs

questions.reveal: Both systems run until the switch, so cancelling the old one never puts her bookings at risk.
